summary:
I closed T1 to T5 in the tools at P/n-tools/tools, branch ntools, HEAD d6eabfc. That is 9 commits on 7d5dab2, status clean, no trailers.

- **Re-key:** the four ports' records went through rekey.js. Nothing was lost: hand records 148/200/236/174 in, 150/204/239/173 out; 0 conflicts, 0 unsourced, 0 hand entries not carried. A second run printed "already keyed".
- **Self-test:** 231 controls, 0 failed, 1 moved. The moved one is the sentence round's own go-tut-step4-dropped [scratch]. There are 28 new controls.
- **T6:** P/results/s3c-sfix-verify.txt does not exist, so T6 passes to the engineer who freezes.

Each reviewer attack that belongs to the tools now fails in the one command:
- the dropped shared sentence: lua, perl and swift, both modes;
- the depluralising helper (purity);
- perl `prints: record`;
- ocaml `keys: member` and swift `entityBy: Name`, in the reviewed mode only, because the OLD page agrees with them;
- a generation that throws, and a short regeneration.

I added a printed-call check, callcheck.js, to the one command. It catches 6 of the reviewers' 10 changed examples and finds nothing on the real pages of all thirteen languages.

**The thirteen languages at d6eabfc** (reviewed mode, against P/v33p/sdkgen and P/v33p/out):
- **PASS:** py, c, zig, clojure, rust.
- **FAIL on openings my changes create:** ts, go, elixir, rb (listed below).
- **FAIL on the sentence round's false-verdict classes and on openings:** perl, swift, ocaml, lua. Perl also still fails on its 14 recorded defects, on purpose.

Every opening is listed per language for a person to decide. I changed no decision in any hand record.

items.item: T2 a language alone in its result style has an absent list
items.does:
When no reference shares the language's style, its absent list is the style-independent sentences: those every reference prints in a variation, whatever its style. The absent file names its basis.
How a style-independent sentence is told from a style-bound one: a sentence a style branch prints (runtimeprose.ts returnClause, failsSentence, carries; the result-style step comments of ReadmeQuick.ts) is printed only by the references of that style. The nine references cover five styles (throw ts; pair go; raise py, clojure, elixir, rb; errslot c; union zig, rust), so a style-bound sentence is in no all-reference intersection. For a language whose style has references, the new list is a subset of the old one, so nothing changes for it.
Consequence: ts, go and c are each alone in their style among the references, so they now get the list too (openings below).

items.does:
Two additions:
- A new 'name surgery' check: an anchored replace holding a letter (`.replace(/s$/, '')`), a negative slice or substr on a name-like receiver, a suffix or prefix test on 1 to 6 letters. It applies to Syntax and Naming line by line, so to every helper either file defines.
- What a Naming hook imports from its own language's directory is followed into its definition and the local functions that definition calls. The same naming rules apply there: pluralisation, name surgery, reserved list, inline reserved test. A rule inside a helper that a non-README component also calls is the code generator's own rule; it is reported as accepted with that reason, not open.
On the thirteen: 0 open. Helpers followed include goVarName (go, hook-only), cVarName and rustVarName (shared with the generator; their reserved lists accepted as the generator's).

items.item: T4 an enumerated fact is judged or said not to be
items.does:
Why the three passed (read in the old attestEnums):
- The units a value 'selected' were every unit any same-value reference printed and no other-value reference printed. That is mostly text the fact has nothing to do with: 391 of 748 units for swift entityBy, 578 of 736 for ocaml keys.
- One identical OLD pair among them attested the fact.

Now the sheet uses a minimal pair. enumgen.js regenerates the language's pages with that one fact set in memory to each other value the clone's providers declare. The clone is not touched; pages are cached in review/enum/ and regenerated when the provider or the shared build changes, about 16 s per value. The units and blocks that differ are what the value selects. Each is set beside its paired OLD unit, comparing only what tells the two values apart: tokens with a letter for prose, exact lines for blocks.

Outcomes:
- ATTESTED when OLD reads as this value more often than as another.
- UNATTESTED otherwise.
- 'not judged' when nothing has an OLD counterpart or no other value exists. Not judged now FAILS until a hand record decides it.
- A value the provider cannot print (perl entityBy module) is skipped and named.

A declared value differing from a hand facts record fails in the reviewed mode. Records keyed with the guard's spelling (ref.facts.entityBy) are accepted.

Finding: ocaml `keys: member` and swift `entityBy: Name` move the port BACK to its OLD page's convention. OLD ocaml reads as member 152 to 0, OLD swift as Name 282 to 0. No comparison with the OLD page can call them wrong; only the reviewed decision can, so they fail in the reviewed mode only. The brief's real case, swift's true 'class' being attested although OLD headed by Name, is now UNATTESTED unless recorded; swift's existing record decides it.

items.item: printed-call check (new, in the one command)
items.does:
callcheck.js reads the code blocks of every NEW page of the language. It checks each call of a runtime member against the declarations the guard's forms read: dist-test/runtimeforms formsOf, view, findDecls, plus overloads anywhere in the language's runtime tree outside feature/ and not private, plus the constructor from layout.ctor. Three findings:
- ARITY: fewer arguments than required, or more than declared. OCaml arguments are juxtaposed atoms, across continuation lines.
- RECEIVER: Lua's `:` against `.` versus the declaration's on; an entity accessor is made on the client instance.
- MEMBER: a call on client, sdk, or a variable bound from the client in the block, naming no runtime member.
On the thirteen: 0 findings. Calls checked: ts 374, go 650, py 386, c 97, zig 761, clojure 0, rust 486, elixir 117, rb 34, perl 30, swift 374, ocaml 481, lua 429.
